title: Linear Inequalities and Their Graphs
_notes: Source of truth for the 1.4 practice set. Every inequality is read by tools/build_exercises.py (ineq_set: the solution set "x op b", with the symbol flipped when the x coefficient is negative), so a flip, a boundary or an open/closed circle can never be wrong. Typed answers (kind "num") carry "derive": smallest-int / largest-int (the smallest / largest whole number that solves q; the circle at the boundary matters), boundary (the number x is compared with), operand:<Property> (q = "A → B"; the number a step divides or multiplies by, sign included) or first-error (q = a student's work, one line per row; the first line whose solutions differ from line 1's). Whole-number mistakes "m": edge (open and closed circle swapped), noflip (the symbol was not flipped), sign (the boundary has the wrong sign), wrongway (the wrong side of the boundary); boundary uses the solve mistakes of 1.3; first-error: last, before, after, first. "match" checks: symbol (phrase → ≥ ≤ > <), graph (inequality → "Open circle at 2, shaded right"), same-solution (inequality → its solution); "multi" checks: flip (moves that flip the symbol), solution:<inequality> (numbers that make it true), valid-from:<inequality> (inequalities with the same solutions). Chips: ADD blue, SUBTRACT purple, MULTIPLY yellow, DIVIDE green, FLIP red (multiplying or dividing by a negative number), DIST yellow, COMBINE green; for a student's work OK green, ERROR red, CARRY ink. See docs/exercises.md.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with its symbol.
exercises.read: Match each phrase with its symbol.
exercises.say_answer: At least is greater than or equal to, at most is less than or equal to, more than is greater than, and fewer than is less than.

pairs.why: At least means this number or more, so the number itself is included.
pairs.say: At least is greater than or equal to: the number itself counts.

pairs.why: At most means this number or less, so the number itself is included.
pairs.say: At most is less than or equal to: the number itself counts.

pairs.why: More than leaves the number itself out.
pairs.say: More than is greater than: the number itself does not count.

pairs.why: Fewer than leaves the number itself out.
pairs.say: Fewer than is less than: the number itself does not count.

exercises.prompt: Match each inequality with its graph.
exercises.read: Match each inequality with its graph.
exercises.say_answer: Greater than shades to the right and less than shades to the left. A circle that is open leaves the number out, and a circle that is filled in keeps it.

pairs.why: Greater than leaves two out, so the circle is open, and it shades to the right.
pairs.say: X is greater than two: an open circle at two, shaded to the right.

pairs.why: Less than or equal to keeps negative one, so the circle is filled in, and it shades to the left.
pairs.say: X is less than or equal to negative one: a closed circle at negative one, shaded to the left.

pairs.why: Greater than or equal to keeps three, so the circle is filled in, and it shades to the right.
pairs.say: X is greater than or equal to three: a closed circle at three, shaded to the right.

pairs.why: Less than leaves negative two out, so the circle is open, and it shades to the left.
pairs.say: X is less than negative two: an open circle at negative two, shaded to the left.

exercises.prompt: Select all the numbers that are solutions of x > 3.
exercises.read: Select all the numbers that are solutions of x is greater than three.
exercises.say_answer: Four, ten, and one hundred are solutions. Three is not, because the circle at three is open, and negative four is on the wrong side.

options.why: Three is the boundary, and x > 3 leaves it out.
options.say: Three. No: three is not greater than three, so the circle at three is open.

options.why: Four is greater than three.
options.say: Four. Yes: four is greater than three.

options.why: Ten is greater than three.
options.say: Ten. Yes: ten is greater than three.

options.why: Negative four is less than three, so it is on the wrong side.
options.say: Negative four. No: negative four is less than three, on the wrong side of the circle.

options.why: One hundred is greater than three.
options.say: One hundred. Yes: one hundred is greater than three.

exercises.prompt: Select all the moves that make you flip the symbol.
exercises.read: Select all the moves that make you flip the symbol.
exercises.say_answer: Dividing by negative four and multiplying by negative one flip the symbol. Adding, subtracting, or dividing by a positive number never does.

options.why: Dividing by a negative number flips the symbol.
options.say: Divide both sides by negative four. Yes: dividing by a negative number flips the symbol.

options.why: Multiplying by a negative number flips the symbol.
options.say: Multiply both sides by negative one. Yes: multiplying by a negative number flips the symbol.

options.why: Adding a negative number does not flip anything: only multiplying or dividing does.
options.say: Add negative three to both sides. No: adding never flips the symbol, even when the number is negative.

options.why: Five is positive, so the symbol stays.
options.say: Divide both sides by five. No: five is positive, so the symbol stays.

options.why: Subtracting never flips the symbol.
options.say: Subtract six from both sides. No: subtracting never flips the symbol.

exercises.prompt: What is the smallest whole number that solves it? Type it.
exercises.read: What is the smallest whole number that solves two x minus one is greater than seven?
say: Add one to both sides, by the addition property. Two x is greater than eight.
Divide both sides by two, by the division property. X is greater than four. Four itself is not included, so the smallest whole number is five.

wrong.why: Four is not a solution: x > 4 leaves four out, because the circle is open.
The boundary is four, not negative four.
wrong.say: give the boundary the wrong sign

wrong.why: Three is on the wrong side: x > 4 means the numbers to the right of four.

exercises.prompt: Starting from −2x < 10, which of these could be the next line? Select all that apply.
exercises.read: Starting from negative two x is less than ten, which of these could be the next line? Choose all that apply.
exercises.say_answer: Three lines follow: x is greater than negative five, two x is greater than negative ten, and negative x is less than five. Each one keeps the same solutions.

options.why: Both sides were divided by −2, and the symbol was flipped.
options.say: X is greater than negative five. Yes: both sides were divided by negative two, and the symbol was flipped.

options.why: Dividing by −2 flips the symbol, and this line did not flip it.
options.say: X is less than negative five. No: dividing by negative two flips the symbol, and this line did not.

options.why: Both sides were multiplied by −1, and the symbol was flipped.
options.say: Two x is greater than negative ten. Yes: both sides were multiplied by negative one, and the symbol was flipped.

options.why: Both sides were divided by 2: the number is positive, so the symbol stays.
options.say: Negative x is less than five. Yes: both sides were divided by two, which is positive, so the symbol stays.

options.why: The boundary has the wrong sign.
options.say: X is greater than five. No: the boundary should be negative five, not five.

exercises.prompt: What number were both sides divided by? Type it, with its sign.
exercises.read: In this step, negative four x is greater than or equal to twenty becomes x is less than or equal to negative five. What number were both sides divided by?
say: X is multiplied by negative four, so divide both sides by negative four, and flip the symbol. X is less than or equal to negative five.

wrong.why: Dividing by four would keep the symbol. The step divides by negative four, which is why the symbol flips.
Negative five is the new right side. The number taken away from x is negative four.
wrong.say: copy the result of the step

wrong.why: Twenty is the old right side. The number both sides are divided by is negative four.
wrong.say: copy the number on the other side

exercises.prompt: What is the largest whole number that solves it? Type it.
exercises.read: What is the largest whole number that solves five minus two x is greater than negative three?
say: Subtract five from both sides, by the subtraction property. Negative two x is greater than negative eight.
Divide both sides by negative two, and flip the symbol. X is less than four. Four is not included, so the largest whole number is three.

wrong.why: Four is not a solution: x < 4 leaves four out, because the circle is open.
Without the flip you get x > 4, which has no largest number. Dividing by a negative number flips the symbol.
The boundary is four, not negative four.
wrong.say: give the boundary the wrong sign

exercises.prompt: Which line of the student's work is the first one that is wrong? Type its number: the first line is line 1.
exercises.read: A student's work is on the screen, line one at the top. Which line is the first one that is wrong?
say: The student distributed negative three, but negative three times negative two is positive six, not negative six. So line two is wrong.
The next step adds six to both sides. That is fine on its own, but it carries the error.
Dividing by negative three flips the symbol, so this step is fine on its own too, but it carries the error.

wrong.why: Line four is only where the wrong answer shows up. The mistake happened earlier.
Line three is fine on its own: adding six to both sides is allowed.
wrong.say: blame the line after the mistake

wrong.why: Line one is the inequality the student was given.

exercises.prompt: Select all the numbers that are solutions of −3x + 4 ≤ 13.
exercises.read: Select all the numbers that are solutions of negative three x plus four is less than or equal to thirteen.
exercises.say_answer: Negative three, zero, and two are solutions: the solutions are x greater than or equal to negative three. Negative four and negative five give more than thirteen.

options.why: −3(−4) + 4 = 16, which is more than 13.
options.say: Negative four. No: negative three times negative four is twelve, plus four is sixteen, which is more than thirteen.
Negative three. Yes: negative three times negative three is nine, plus four is thirteen, and thirteen is less than or equal to thirteen.

options.why: −3(0) + 4 = 4, which is less than 13.
options.say: Zero. Yes: negative three times zero is zero, plus four is four, which is less than thirteen.

options.why: −3(2) + 4 = −2, which is less than 13.
options.say: Two. Yes: negative three times two is negative six, plus four is negative two, which is less than thirteen.

options.why: −3(−5) + 4 = 19, which is more than 13.
options.say: Negative five. No: negative three times negative five is fifteen, plus four is nineteen, which is more than thirteen.

exercises.prompt: Match each inequality with its solution.
exercises.read: Match each inequality with its solution.
exercises.say_answer: Each solution comes from undoing the operations. Dividing or multiplying by a negative number flips the symbol, so negative three x is greater than or equal to twelve becomes x is less than or equal to negative four.

pairs.why: Subtract 4 from both sides: the symbol stays.
pairs.say: X plus four is less than ten. Subtract four from both sides: x is less than six.

pairs.why: Divide both sides by 3: the symbol stays.
pairs.say: Three x is greater than or equal to twelve. Divide by three: x is greater than or equal to four.

pairs.why: Divide both sides by −3, and flip the symbol.
pairs.say: Negative three x is greater than or equal to twelve. Divide by negative three, and flip the symbol: x is less than or equal to negative four.

pairs.why: Multiply both sides by −1, and flip the symbol.
pairs.say: Negative x is less than two. Multiply by negative one, and flip the symbol: x is greater than negative two.

exercises.prompt: What is the smallest whole number that solves it? Type it.
exercises.read: What is the smallest whole number that solves four minus x is less than two x plus thirteen?
say: Add x to both sides, by the addition property of equality. Four is less than three x plus thirteen.
Subtract thirteen from both sides, by the subtraction property. Negative nine is less than three x.
Divide both sides by three, by the division property. Negative three is less than x, so x is greater than negative three. Negative three is not included, so the smallest whole number is negative two.

wrong.why: Negative three is not a solution: the circle at negative three is open.
Moving the x terms to the left gives negative three x is less than nine. Dividing by negative three flips the symbol, so x is greater than negative three, not less.
The boundary is negative three, not three.
wrong.say: give the boundary the wrong sign

exercises.prompt: What is the largest whole number that solves it? Type it.
exercises.read: What is the largest whole number that solves three minus two times the quantity x plus one, is greater than nine?
say: Distribute the negative two: negative two times x is negative two x, and negative two times one is negative two. Three minus two x minus two is greater than nine.
Combine three and negative two: that is one. One minus two x is greater than nine.
Subtract one from both sides, by the subtraction property. Negative two x is greater than eight.
Divide both sides by negative two, and flip the symbol. X is less than negative four. Negative four is not included, so the largest whole number is negative five.

wrong.why: Negative four is not a solution: x < −4 leaves it out, because the circle is open.
Without the flip you get x > −4, which has no largest number. Dividing by a negative number flips the symbol.
The boundary is negative four, not four.
wrong.say: give the boundary the wrong sign

exercises.prompt: Which line of the student's work is the first one that is wrong? Type its number: the first line is line 1.
exercises.read: A student's work is on the screen, line one at the top. Which line is the first one that is wrong?
say: The first step adds two x to both sides, by the addition property. That is allowed, so line two is fine.
The second step adds eight to both sides. That is allowed too, so line three is fine.

The third step divides both sides by six. Six is positive, so the symbol stays: eighteen is greater than or equal to six x becomes three is greater than or equal to x. The student wrote x is greater than or equal to three instead, so line four is wrong.
The last step swaps the sides, which is fine on its own, but it carries the error.

wrong.why: Line five is only where the wrong answer shows up. The mistake happened earlier.
Line three is fine: adding eight to both sides is allowed.
wrong.say: blame the line before the mistake

wrong.why: Line one is the inequality the student was given.
